1.title: Journal I
paragraphs: I awoke this morning with the distinct and most unwelcome impression that some portion of myself had been mislaid. I made at once a careful examination of my person and faculties, yet discovered nothing to account for so singular a conviction. My pulse was regular, my hand steady, and my memory, so far as I could test it, unimpaired.
And yet the impression persists.

I record this after a trying passage from the lower workings. There I was set upon by the animated dead and by creatures of living flame, whose heat I felt even at a distance. Yet the danger of that passage does not account for the more singular distress that has followed me from it.
It is not that I recall the loss of any particular thing, but that I am sensible of an absence where no absence ought to be. The deficiency does not reside in the body.
I have quit the lower depths in haste, though I cannot yet name the agency that pressed me upward. I have the sensation in these caverns of being watched by something that waits for sleep.
I shall observe whether it recurs upon the next occasion of sleep.
I hear it again beyond the camp. It has found me.
I must go at once.

2.title: Journal II
paragraphs: The pursuit has not abated. I have passed through chambers where the dead stir at the edge of torchlight, and where the air itself seems to churn before the creatures of flame appear. Their coming is often preceded by a dry heat upon the face and a faint crackling, as of timber burned at some unseen hearth.

In former nights I took refuge beside the pale blooms, believing their light served as a barrier against the things that prowled beyond it. I cannot deny that the creatures draw back from them. Yet each morning I wake with that same curious vacancy, as though some small part of me has failed to rise with the rest.
I am not prepared to abandon the blooms. Without them I do not think I should survive the night.

Still, I have begun to mistrust their mercy. The nearest flower seemed brighter at dawn than it had been at dusk, and its cup held a faint warmth, though no flame had touched it. When I placed my hand near the petals, I felt not comfort, but a peculiar answering sensation, as if some portion of myself had been recognized.
It may be exhaustion. It may be terror lending form to fancy.
And yet I begin to fear that these blooms do not merely stand between me and the darkness. They may be taking something from me while I sleep, and keeping it after I am driven onward.

3.title: Journal III
paragraphs: The passages behind me have narrowed into brick corridors and broken courts. The walls groan at intervals, as though the whole place suffers under some inward pressure. Since dusk I have heard ordered steps, halting and resuming together, as if the marchers obey some command I cannot hear.

I have slept beside the blooms because they offered the only mercy left to me. They held back the night long enough for me to rise again, and each morning I woke with less of myself than I had carried into sleep.
There is no longer room for the comfort of uncertainty.

The flowers have not sheltered my soul. They have taken it by degrees, portion after portion, until the heart within me feels like a room from which every familiar object has been removed. I was grateful for each waking, and so I did not understand the price.
As I gaze upon the bloom before me, I feel no outrage. Outrage belongs to men who still possess themselves. What remains in me is colder, poorer, and terribly calm.
Something advances beyond the garden.

I will leave the shelter and take up my letter, though I scarcely know what hand remains to carry it. I must pass the garden and make for the meadow below, where the steps descend through the grass and the open sky may yet receive my appeal.
If I am taken there, I do not know whether my body shall ever be found.
If my letter is borne away, I pray some living soul may read it.
